transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-10-09
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Torres (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Elliot Zhang (CTO, Hypernova), Maya Patel (Lead ML Engineer, Hypernova), Arjun Rao (Infra, Hypernova), Sana Kim (PM, Hypernova)

Summary: quick discovery to align on latency p95 targets, concurrency, streaming behavior, and what metrics we need for a pilot. Customer wants low-latency streaming for a multi-tenant real-time product and is weighing host/dedicated/private options.

Topics: p95 targets, concurrency & burst, continuous streaming vs chunking, token/sec bench mark, KV cache/prefix caching, quantization tradeoffs, security (SOC2/KMS/VPC).

[00:00:05] Jamie (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jamie, AE at Redwood, and with me is Priya our SE. Quick round intro?
[00:00:18] Elliot (Hypernova CTO): Elliot here. We're building a live summarization product. Our latency targets are strict, um, so wanted to see if Redwood can hit p95 of ~200ms for short prompts and also how throughput scales.
[00:00:30] Maya (Hypernova): Hi, Maya. I run the model infra and will be running the bench. We'll share prompt sets after.
[00:00:40] Priya (Redwood SE): great, thanks. Can you confirm traffic shape? avg tokens per request and concurrency?
[00:00:50] Maya: typical prompt is 40-80 tokens, responses ~60 tokens. P95 goal 200ms for the whole response, and we need to support 200 concurrent users during peak with bursts to 400.
[00:01:05] Arjun (Hypernova): we're on AWS, VPC, prefer private peering but open to hosted if data retention/SGs are ok. Encryption with customer-managed KMS is a must.
[00:01:20] Priya: ok, good. A couple of things to call out: p95 is sensitive to both model size and streaming behavior. Are you planning streaming token-by-token to clients or returning full payloads?
[00:01:35] Maya: streaming; clients require partial deltas. So token/sec and first-byte latency matter.
[00:01:44] Jamie: perfect. So the two axes are first-byte latency (startup) and end-to-end p95. For streaming, p95 for first token and p95 for_completion differ.

[00:02:10] Priya: How strict is the 200ms — is that first token or full 60-token response?
[00:02:17] Elliot: goal is 200ms p95 for the first token and sub-600ms for full 60-token responses ideally. If that's impossible on larger models we'll trade to smaller model variants.
[00:02:28] Priya: makes sense. For Hosted, we typically see first-token p95 in the 80-180ms range on curated small-medium models with streaming enabled, but your throughput and concurrency will shift that. For Dedicated you get more predictable p95 at scale because you reserve GPU pools and have isolation. Private has network hops depending on VPC peering.

[00:03:05] Maya: can you give an example token/sec numbers we should expect at 200 conc?
[00:03:12] Priya: rough calc: if each response is 60 tokens and you have 200 concurrent streaming sessions, and each session generates ~10 tokens/sec on average, that's 2k tokens/sec. But if your clients request many short outputs concurrently burst to 400, sustained token/sec could be 4k. If you run batching and prefix cache you can drive down GPU token cost and increase throughput to tens of k tokens/sec in Dedicated setups.
[00:03:40] Jamie: we also recommend KV caching for repeated prefixes to reduce per-token latency. Note: some docs auto transcribed 'KV cash' in older logs, ha.

[00:04:00] Elliot: we plan to do a mix - a lot of repeated system prompts. That would help. How do quantization choices affect p95?
[00:04:10] Priya: 4-bit quant helps throughput and memory, sometimes increases latency slightly per token due to dequant steps but overall usually improves token/sec. But key is kernel selection in the runtime; some kernels are optimized for streaming. We can run both quantized and fp16 in bench.

[00:05:00] Arjun: networking — if we go Private, what's network egress and TLS termination look like? Also SSO for RBAC?
[00:05:08] Jamie: Private supports customer-managed VPC peering, TLS to your endpoint, and KMS for key management; SAML SSO + SCIM supported for RBAC. We'll send the SOC2 pack and network diagram.

[00:06:00] Maya: ok, bench specifics — we need a run that measures p95 at target concs: 50, 100, 200, 400, and also token/sec sustained for 10m windows, plus 95/99 for first token and completion. Can Redwood run that in-hosted or do we need Dedicated?
[00:06:20] Priya: we can run initial synthetic benches on Hosted to show relative numbers, but for production-accurate numbers Dedicated or Private with reserved GPU pools is better. For Hosted we might see noisy p95 under high conc because of noisy neighbors.

[00:07:00] Elliot: timeline — we want pilot in 3 weeks. What do you need from us?
[00:07:06] Priya: prompt set, concurrency matrix, example client behavior (stream TPS), and network egress constraints. We'll propose bench script and config.

[00:07:30] Jamie: pricing question — how does Dedicated pricing work for reserved capacity vs burst?
[00:07:36] Jamie (continues): Dedicated is commit-based monthly. You can reserve a baseline and configure burst to shared pool with overage billing. We'll email the pricing matrix.

[00:08:10] Maya: any known customers doing sub-200ms p95 for first byte at 200 conc?
[00:08:17] Priya: yes, in multimedia real-time summarization we have customers hitting ~120ms first-byte p95 on Dedicated with prefix caching and optimized kernels; though payload sizes and model choices vary. We'll share anonymized case study.

[00:09:00] Arjun: what about token/sec optimizations — does Redwood support batching across tenants or only same-tenant batching?
[00:09:08] Priya: supports workload-aware batching that can batch similar requests; for multi-tenant we enforce isolation policies, but batching can be within a dedicated pool. For Hosted we do cross-tenant batching with strict privacy controls, but Dedicated gives you more control.

[00:10:00] Maya: can you walk through p95 latency components?
[00:10:05] Priya: sure — components: client network + TLS handshake (if not already open), routing/routing policy, model warm/cold start, prefix KV cache hit, runtime per-token kernels, and final assembly + transport. For streaming the first token is mostly network + model init + runtime first-step.

[00:11:00] Elliot: warm starts — do you recommend pinned model instances for low p95?
[00:11:07] Priya: yes. Keep model pinned in memory on Dedicated to avoid cold starts. Hosted has warm pools but under extreme scale you can get evictions.

[00:12:00] Maya: about the benchmark — we want token/sec measured end-to-end and also raw decoder token/sec on GPU. Can Redwood provide both metrics?
[00:12:09] Priya: yes, we emit token/sec at runtime, GPU utilization, and end-to-end latency histograms. We'll instrument the bench to provide both. We'll share the bench spreadsheet link after the call (note: link placeholder: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/hypernova).

[00:13:30] Jamie: security questions?
[00:13:34] Arjun: SOC2 status, audit logs, retention, data residency.
[00:13:40] Jamie: we are SOC2 Type II certified, we provide audit logs, and retention is configurable. For Private on-prem we can support air-gapped deployments. We'll include the security pack.

[00:15:00] Maya: edge cases — streaming interruptions and reconnects. How does Redwood preserve KV cache during reconnects?
[00:15:08] Priya: cache is per-session and can be rehydrated if you use our session tokens. For strict requirements we recommend session affinity with Dedicated.

[00:18:00] Elliot: are there limits to concurrent streams per model instance?
[00:18:06] Priya: depends on model throughput and GPU ram; e.g., for a medium model you might get ~50 concurrent streaming sessions per GPU with good batch packing; larger models reduce that. We'll provide guidance per model.

[00:22:00] Maya: can you quantify p95 tradeoffs when enabling quantization?
[00:22:05] Priya: in our tests quantization (4-bit) improved token/sec by ~1.8-2x but added ~10-40ms to per-token latency depending on kernel. Net effect is usually positive for throughput-conscious workloads. We'll validate with your prompt set.

[00:28:00] Arjun: network diagram question — if we do VPC peering, what's the egress port list we need?
[00:28:08] Jamie: we'll send a minimal set plus optional ones. Also note that some on-prem firewalls need keepalives to avoid TLS idle close which can impact first-byte.

[00:33:00] Maya: ok let's spell out acceptance criteria for the pilot.
[00:33:05] Elliot: acceptance: first-byte p95 <= 200ms, completion p95 <= 600ms for 60-token responses at 200 concurrent sustained for a 10m window; error rate < 1% and token/sec sustain >= 4k.
[00:33:25] Priya: captured. We'll design the bench to measure those and instrument histograms.

[00:40:00] Jamie: logistics — we'll propose two run types: synthetic (hosted) for quick numbers and production-accurate (dedicated/private) with your prompt set. Which do you want first?
[00:40:10] Elliot: synthetic first to surface glaring issues, then dedicated run. Aim to start synthetic next week.

[00:44:00] Maya: any blockers on our side?
[00:44:05] Priya: just need prompt set, concurrency matrix, and network access rules. Also confirm if you require customer-managed KMS.

[00:50:00] Jamie: recap and next steps — we'll send pricing/contract, SOC2 and network diagram, bench plan and link, and schedule the synthetic run.
[00:50:18] Elliot: sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[00:50:25] Maya: thanks.
[00:50:30] Jamie: thanks, bye.

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings (KV cash, P ninety five). Shared artifacts: pricing matrix (will attach in follow-up), SOC2 pack (link in follow-up), bench spreadsheet (redwood.example.com/benchmarks/hypernova).
